q: Did games with smaller crowds coincide with smaller national TV audiences in 2025 and 2026?
title: MLB attendance and national TV audiences, 2025-2026
cited: Yes, games with smaller crowds tended to have smaller national TV audiences, but a crowd that was small for its own park did not clearly mean a smaller audience (table: crowd_tv_headline). Across team-seasons, teams with higher average home attendance also tended to have larger average national TV audiences (correlation 0.51, n = 56, range 0.29 to 0.68) (table: team_crowd_tv). This is consistent with team-level factors such as popularity and market size, but the data does not show that one causes the other.

q: What drives MLB attendance?

chart.title: Game factors associated with attendance
labels: Games with a closed roof or dome
chart.note: Each bar is compared with its own baseline: Friday for days, August for months, and the average opponent for opponents. Only the largest clear associations are shown.

title: What drives MLB attendance, 2024 to 2026
cited:
Winning games and welcoming back past crowds are the strongest drivers of MLB season attendance, while home openers and premium opponents like the Dodgers spark the biggest single-game spikes.

### Season-Level Drivers

Sixteen additional wins in a 162-game season was associated with a 8.8% increase in season-level attendance, making team performance and prior crowds the strongest predictors of how many fans a team will draw (table: model_coefficients; query: Q2). Ten percent higher crowds over the prior two years coincided with a 8.0% increase in season attendance (table: model_coefficients; query: Q2). By contrast, ten percent larger metro populations were associated with just a 0.2% increase, which was not a clear effect (table: model_coefficients; query: Q2).

### Game-by-Game Drivers

Home openers coincided with the largest single-game increase, associated with a 69.1% jump in attendance (table: model_coefficients; query: Q1). The Los Angeles Dodgers were associated with a 25.0% increase compared to the average opponent, followed by the New York Yankees at 15.7%, the Chicago Cubs at 13.1%, and the Philadelphia Phillies at 9.5% (table: model_coefficients; query: Q1). On the field, sixteen additional wins over a 162-game season was associated with a 4.7% increase in game-by-game attendance (table: model_coefficients; query: Q4).

Saturday games were associated with a 8.8% increase compared to Fridays, while weekday games saw drops compared to Fridays: Monday games were associated with a 21.8% decrease, Wednesday games a 20.6% decrease, Tuesday games a 18.9% decrease, and Thursday games a 16.6% decrease (table: model_coefficients; query: Q1). March and April games were associated with a 10.9% decrease compared to August, while July games coincided with a 4.2% increase (table: model_coefficients; query: Q1, Q4). Indoor games or domes were associated with a 7.0% decrease, and precipitation coincided with a 5.7% decrease (table: model_coefficients; query: Q1).

### Model Fit

The team-level model explained most of the variation in season attendance (0.9; 86 team-seasons) (table: model_fit; query: Q6). The game-level model also showed strong fit, capturing most of the variation in game attendance (0.8; 7,205 games) (table: model_fit; query: Q6). It also accounted for a solid portion of the variation within the same park in a single season (0.4) (table: model_fit; query: Q6). The model's prediction error was low, with a cross-validation error of 0.2 compared to a baseline of 0.3 (table: model_fit; query: Q6).
